import { Callout, Code, CodeBlock, H2, Prose } from "../../components/content"; import { MathBlock } from "../../components/content/Math.jsx"; const content = { title: "Combinatorial Optimization & Approximation Algorithms", readTime: "~44 min", content: () =>

1. The question: choose the best feasible combination

Many important decisions are discrete: which deliveries go on which route, which experiments to run under a budget, which workers cover shifts, which features to select, or which facilities to open. Combinatorial optimisation chooses the best feasible combination from an enormous set of possibilities. The difficulty is not writing the objective; it is that the number of combinations often grows exponentially. {`\\min_{x\\in\\mathcal{X}} f(x) \\qquad \\text{subject to }g_j(x)\\leq0,\\;x_i\\in\\{0,1\\}`} Binary decision variables are a common language: x_i = 1 means select item i, assign a job, or include an edge. Feasibility constraints encode the rules you may not break; the objective encodes what "best" means. A fast but infeasible solution is not an approximate solution—it is simply unusable.

2. Learn to recognise the problem family

Some discrete problems have efficient exact algorithms: shortest paths, minimum spanning trees, maximum flow, and bipartite matching are classic examples. Others, such as travelling salesperson, set cover, general integer programming, and many scheduling variants, are NP-hard. NP-hard does not mean hopeless; it means a polynomial-time exact algorithm is not known for all instances, so structure, solvers, approximation, or heuristics become important. Modelling comes first. A routing problem can be a shortest path, a vehicle-routing problem, or a time-window scheduling problem depending on capacities, multiple vehicles, service times, and constraints. Calling everything "TSP" is a great way to solve the wrong problem beautifully.

3. Exact methods still matter

Use exhaustive search only for tiny instances or as a correctness oracle. Dynamic programming exploits overlapping subproblems, branch-and-bound prunes partial solutions using optimistic bounds, and mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) lets modern solvers combine cutting planes, branching, and presolve. Constraint programming is often excellent when the problem is rich in logical or scheduling constraints. Start by solving representative instances exactly or with a trusted solver. It establishes a baseline, reveals binding constraints, and lets you measure how much quality a faster approximation or heuristic actually gives up.

4. Approximation algorithms come with a worst-case contract

For a minimisation problem, an alpha-approximation always returns a feasible solution whose cost is at most alpha times the optimal cost. For maximisation, it returns at least a 1/alpha fraction of optimal value. The guarantee is about the worst case, not a prediction that every real instance will be exactly alpha times worse. {`f(x_{\\mathrm{alg}})\\leq\\alpha f(x^*)\\quad\\text{for minimisation}, \\qquad f(x_{\\mathrm{alg}})\\geq\\frac{1}{\\alpha}f(x^*)\\quad\\text{for maximisation}`} Guarantees make approximation algorithms valuable in systems where solution quality has contractual, financial, or safety implications. A heuristic may be faster or better on your data, but without a proof it can fail arbitrarily badly on an adversarial or shifted case.

5. Greedy set cover: fast, useful, and not always optimal

In set cover, choose as few candidate sets as possible to cover every required item. The greedy rule repeatedly chooses the set that covers the most currently uncovered items. It has a logarithmic approximation guarantee, yet the small example below shows why "greedy" does not mean "optimal": choosing the largest first set forces three choices, while two smaller sets cover everything. {`from itertools import combinations universe = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6} candidates = { "A": {1, 2, 3, 4}, "B": {1, 2, 5}, "C": {3, 4, 6}, } covered, greedy = set(), [] while covered != universe: name, new_items = max(candidates.items(), key=lambda item: len(item[1] - covered)) greedy.append(name) covered |= new_items optimal = next( combo for size in range(1, len(candidates) + 1) for combo in combinations(candidates, size) if set().union(*(candidates[name] for name in combo)) == universe ) print(greedy) print(list(optimal))`} {`['A', 'B', 'C'] ['B', 'C']`} Greedy set cover is still valuable because it is simple and has a proven bound of roughly ln(n) + 1 for n covered elements. The point of the example is to set expectations: inspect quality against an exact baseline on samples rather than assuming a locally best move creates a globally best plan.

6. Relaxation and rounding create many strong algorithms

A common strategy relaxes binary decisions to continuous values, solves the easier linear or convex problem, then rounds the result back to a legal discrete choice. The relaxation supplies a bound; careful rounding preserves feasibility and yields an approximation ratio. Primal-dual methods and randomised rounding are powerful variants of this idea. For example, an LP relaxation may assign an item half to two facilities, which is not physically legal. A rounding scheme converts that fractional plan into actual assignments while tracking how much objective cost and constraint violation can grow. Naively rounding at 0.5 often breaks capacity, coverage, or fairness constraints, so the rounding procedure is part of the algorithm.

7. Heuristics, metaheuristics, and ML-assisted optimisation

Local search, simulated annealing, genetic algorithms, and learned heuristics can produce excellent solutions quickly for large, structured instances. Use them when an exact solve is too slow and a formal approximation is unavailable or too conservative. Their evaluation must include feasibility rate, objective distribution across random seeds, runtime, sensitivity to input changes, and comparison with solver baselines—not only a best-ever run. ML can predict costs, prune candidate actions, or propose warm starts, but an accurate predictor does not ensure an optimal decision. Optimisation amplifies errors near constraints and thresholds. Keep a feasibility checker and a safe fallback in the deployment loop.

8. A responsible workflow

Define the decision variables, objective units, hard constraints, and uncertainty before choosing an algorithm. Identify the problem family and solve small or representative cases exactly. Select an exact solver, approximation, or heuristic based on scale and required guarantees. Validate feasibility independently, stress-test edge cases and data shift, and monitor realised cost—not only the proxy objective. If decisions affect people, include fairness, service-level, and override constraints explicitly rather than hoping they emerge from a scalar objective. Formulate a weekly staff-scheduling problem with binary variables. List three hard constraints, two competing objective terms, and one uncertainty source. Which exact or approximate method would you try first, and what baseline would you use to decide whether it is good enough?
